c: Voltage comes from chemistry

A battery cell produces a voltage set by the materials inside it, not by its size. An alkaline cell gives about 1.5 volts whether it is a small AAA or a large D. A nickel metal hydride rechargeable gives about 1.2. A lithium-ion cell gives a nominal 3.6 or 3.7. A lead-acid cell gives about 2.1, and six in series make the familiar 12 volt car battery. To get more voltage, cells are stacked in series. Size affects only how long the cell lasts.
Capacity

Capacity is measured in amp hours or milliamp hours: current multiplied by time. A good AA alkaline holds roughly 2,000 to 3,000 milliamp hours at low drain. A common cylindrical lithium-ion cell holds 2,500 to 3,500. A coin cell of the CR2032 type holds only about 220. To compare batteries of different voltages fairly, multiply capacity by voltage to get watt hours, which is the stored energy.
Voltage sags as you use it

A battery's voltage is not constant. An alkaline cell starts above 1.5 volts and declines steadily toward 1.0 as it empties, so devices that need a firm 1.5 volts quit while much of the energy remains. Lithium-ion holds a flatter voltage through most of its discharge, from 4.2 volts when full to about 3.0 when empty. This is why a fuel gauge based on voltage alone works tolerably for alkaline cells and poorly for lithium ones.
Internal resistance

Every battery behaves as if it had a small resistor in series with it. When you draw current, some voltage is lost across that internal resistance, and the battery warms. Alkaline cells have fairly high internal resistance, so they perform poorly in high-drain devices such as camera flashes, delivering a fraction of their rated capacity. Rechargeable cells have much lower internal resistance and handle heavy loads far better, despite their lower nominal voltage.
The C rate

Charge and discharge currents are often quoted relative to capacity. A rate of 1C means a current that would empty the battery in one hour. For a 2,000 milliamp hour cell, 1C is 2 amps, and half that rate is 1 amp. Each cell type has limits. Ordinary lithium-ion cells are typically charged at half C to 1C. Cells built for power tools and drones can discharge at 10C or more. Exceeding the rating overheats the cell.
Lithium needs respect

Lithium-ion cells store a great deal of energy in a small space, several times more per kilogram than lead-acid. They must be kept within strict limits. Charged above about 4.2 volts, discharged below about 2.5 to 3, short-circuited or punctured, they can overheat and catch fire. Nearly every pack includes a protection circuit, and they need a charger designed for the chemistry. Do not charge them when they are below freezing. A swollen cell should be retired at once.
Making them last

Rechargeable batteries wear out with use and with time. For lithium-ion, heat is the main enemy, followed by being held at full charge. A laptop kept plugged in at 100 percent in a warm room ages faster than one cycled between 30 and 80 percent. For long storage, leave lithium cells at around half charge in a cool place. Nickel metal hydride cells of the low self-discharge type hold most of their charge for a year on the shelf.
Choosing for a project

For a device that sips power for months, such as a remote control or a clock, alkaline cells are cheap and simple. For anything used daily with moderate drain, low self-discharge nickel metal hydride cells pay for themselves quickly. For compact, high-energy designs, lithium-ion or lithium polymer with a proper charging and protection module is standard. For large amounts of energy where weight does not matter, lead-acid remains cheap and forgiving.
Why it usually fails

Telling someone their presentation was weak, or that they need to be more professional, gives them nothing to work with. They know you are displeased. They do not know what to change. Because the remark is about them and not about anything in particular, it feels like a judgement of character, and people defend their character. The usual result is resentment and no improvement. Vague praise fails in a similar way: pleasant and uninformative.
Describe the behaviour

Useful feedback names something the person did that an observer could have seen or heard. Not you were disorganized, which is a conclusion, but the report arrived two days after the date we agreed. Not you are careless, but there were four arithmetic errors in the summary table. A description of behaviour can be discussed and corrected. A label can only be accepted or rejected, and it will nearly always be rejected.
Situation, behaviour, impact

One widely taught structure has three parts. First state the situation: when and where. Then the behaviour: what the person did. Then the impact: the effect it had on you, the team or the work. In Tuesday's client meeting, you interrupted the client twice while she was describing the problem, and she stopped offering details. Each part is a fact or a first-hand observation. The listener may not like it, and they cannot easily dispute it.
Say it soon

Feedback loses value with every day that passes. The details fade for both of you, and the person may repeat the behaviour in the meantime. Saving up criticism for an annual review is nearly useless, and it arrives as an ambush. The best moment is as soon as you can speak privately and calmly. If you are angry, wait until you are not, since anger turns a description into an accusation, but do not wait a month.
In private, and ask first

Criticism delivered in front of others adds humiliation, and the person will remember that and nothing else. Praise can be public. Correction should not be. It also helps to ask before beginning: may I give you some thoughts on the meeting? The question takes two seconds, gives the other person a moment to prepare and some sense of control, and makes it far more likely that they will listen instead of bracing for a blow.
Look forward

Having described what happened, turn to what should happen next. What would you like them to do differently? Better still, ask what they think. People are more committed to solutions they have proposed themselves. A conversation that ends with a specific change agreed on both sides has succeeded. One that ends with the person merely feeling bad has achieved nothing, however accurate the criticism was.
Praise needs the same precision

Specific positive feedback is as valuable as specific criticism and far rarer. Good job tells someone only that you are pleased. Saying that the way they summarized the three options on one page let the committee decide in ten minutes tells them exactly what to do again. People repeat what they understand to have worked. If you want more of a behaviour, describe it as carefully as you would describe a fault.
Receiving it

The other half of the skill is taking feedback well. When someone criticizes your work, the instinct is to explain or defend. Resist it. Listen to the end. Ask a question to make sure you understand, and ask for an example if none was given. Thank them, since it took some effort to say. You can decide afterwards how much of it you agree with. People who react defensively soon stop being told anything.
Pooling risk

Insurance works by pooling. A thousand households each face a small chance of a house fire in a given year. For any one of them, the loss would be ruinous. For the group, the number of fires is fairly predictable. Each household pays a modest premium, and the pooled money rebuilds the few houses that burn. An unpredictable catastrophe for the individual is turned into a small, certain cost shared by all.
You should expect to lose

Premiums must cover the claims paid out plus the insurer's staff, offices, advertising and profit. So customers as a group pay in more than they get back. Measured purely by expected value, buying insurance is a losing bet. That is not a criticism. You are paying a fee to be rid of a risk you could not bear. The purchase makes sense when the possible loss would wreck your finances and little sense when it would not.
Insure against ruin

The principle that follows is to insure against losses you could not absorb and to carry the rest yourself. A house burning down, a serious illness or injury, being held liable for harming someone else, or the death or disability of a family's earner are all capable of destroying a household's finances. These are worth insuring fully. A cracked phone screen or a failed toaster is an annoyance that savings can cover.
Small policies are poor value

Extended warranties on appliances and electronics, insurance on individual gadgets and similar small policies are generally expensive relative to the risk they cover, since sales commissions and administration absorb much of the premium. Consumer organizations have long advised against most of them. If you decline all such offers and put the money aside, you will almost certainly come out ahead over the years, and you will have the cash for the occasional repair.
Deductibles

The deductible, or excess, is the part of any claim you pay yourself. A higher one lowers the premium, often considerably, because it removes the small claims that are costly for an insurer to process. This is the same principle again. Choose the highest deductible you could comfortably pay from savings, and let the policy protect you against the large losses. An emergency fund and a high deductible work well together.
Problems insurers face

Two difficulties shape every policy. People who know they are at higher risk are keener to buy cover, which pushes up the average cost. Insurers respond with questionnaires, medical checks and exclusions. And people who are insured may take less care, since someone else will pay. Insurers respond with deductibles and conditions. Much of the fine print that irritates customers exists to manage these two problems.
Reading a policy

Three items deserve attention before you buy. The limit is the most the insurer will pay, and it should match the loss you actually face. The exclusions list what is not covered, and floods, earthquakes and wear are commonly left out of standard home policies. The basis of payment says whether you receive what an item would cost to replace or only its depreciated value. Comparing quotes on price alone, without these, compares different products.
A sensible approach

List the events that could seriously damage your finances and check that each is covered up to a realistic amount. For most households, that means health, home or contents, motor liability, and life and disability cover if others depend on your income. Raise deductibles to what you can afford. Decline cover for small things. Review the whole arrangement every couple of years or after any major change in your life, and seek qualified advice when the amounts are large.
What changes on the river

On earlier streets, hands have potential. Draws can arrive and leads can change. On the river all of that is finished. Your hand's value is fixed, and it will either win at showdown or it will not. There is nothing left to protect against and no equity to deny. The only purposes of a river bet are to get called by a worse hand or to make a better hand fold. A bet that does neither is a mistake.
Three categories

Sort your hand into one of three groups. A value hand is strong enough that worse hands will call a bet. A bluff is a hand that cannot win at showdown and can only take the pot by betting. In between are hands with showdown value: good enough to win sometimes when checked, not good enough to be called by worse. These medium hands should usually check. Betting them drives out everything they beat.
In position

When you act last and are checked to, the decision is simple. With a value hand, bet an amount that worse hands will pay. With a hand that has showdown value, check behind and see who wins. With nothing, decide whether your opponent will fold often enough to justify a bluff, given the size you would need. Acting last means you never face a raise after checking, which is one more reason position is worth so much.
Out of position

First to act is harder. If you check a strong hand hoping to raise, the opponent may check behind and you win nothing extra. If you bet a medium hand, you may be raised off it. A common approach is to bet your strong hands and your chosen bluffs, and to check your medium hands planning to call some bets and fold to others. Against aggressive opponents, checking a few strong hands as well keeps them from attacking every check.
Facing a bet

When your opponent bets the river, work out the price. A bet of half the pot means you need to hold the best hand 25 percent of the time. A pot-sized bet means 33 percent. Then estimate, from the way the hand was played, how often this player is bluffing or betting a worse hand for value. If that is more often than the price requires, call. If less, fold. The strength of your own hand matters only relative to their range.
Bluff catchers

A bluff catcher is a hand that beats every bluff and loses to every value bet. Top pair on a board where a flush and a straight have both arrived is a typical example. With such a hand, raising is pointless, and the choice is call or fold. The useful question is whether there are enough missed draws in the opponent's range. If every obvious draw completed on the river, they have few natural bluffs and you should fold more.
Raises mean strength

A river raise is the strongest action in poker. In most games, particularly at low and middle stakes, players almost never raise the river as a bluff. They raise with the nuts or close to it. Folding a good hand to a river raise feels terrible and is usually correct. Over time, the players who pay off river raises with one pair or two pair, just to see it, give back a large part of what they win elsewhere.
Take your time

The river is where pots are biggest and mistakes cost the most. There is no penalty for pausing. Replay the hand from the start: what the opponent did before the flop, how they reacted to each card, what sizes they used. Ask which hands play this way. Then decide. Many expensive errors on the river are made in two seconds by players who would have got it right with twenty.
Voltages as bits

A digital signal carries information as one of two states, high or low, usually written 1 and 0. Physically, these are voltage ranges. In a 5 volt system, a voltage near 5 is high and near zero is low. In a 3.3 volt system, high is near 3.3. Most modern microcontrollers and sensors use 3.3 volts or lower, because lower voltages save power and suit smaller transistors. Older designs and many hobby boards still use 5.
The thresholds

A chip does not require exactly 5 volts or exactly zero. It has thresholds. For a typical 3.3 volt part, anything above about 2 volts is guaranteed to be read as high and anything below about 0.8 volts as low. Between them lies an undefined band where the result is not promised. The gap between what an output delivers and what an input requires is the noise margin, and it is what makes digital circuits tolerant of interference.
Floating inputs

An input pin connected to nothing is not at zero. It is floating. Modern inputs draw almost no current, so the pin's voltage is set by stray electric fields from nearby wires, the mains and even your hand moving past. It drifts unpredictably between high and low. A circuit with a floating input may work on the bench and fail when you lean over it. Every input must be driven to a defined level at all times.
Pull-up and pull-down resistors

The standard cure is a resistor that gently holds the pin at a known level when nothing else is driving it. A pull-up connects the pin to the supply. A pull-down connects it to ground. A push button then needs only to connect the pin to the opposite level when pressed. The usual value is around 10 kilohms: low enough to hold the pin firmly, high enough that little current is wasted while the button is held.
Built-in pull-ups

Most microcontrollers contain optional pull-up resistors on their input pins, switched on in software. They are typically in the range of 20 to 50 kilohms. Enabling one saves an external part. The consequence is that the logic reads backwards from what beginners expect. With a pull-up, the pin reads high when the button is not pressed and low when it is. This arrangement is called active low and is extremely common.
Mixing 5 and 3.3 volts

Connecting parts that run at different voltages needs care in one direction. A 3.3 volt output driving a 5 volt input often works, since 3.3 volts is above the high threshold of many 5 volt inputs, though not all. A 5 volt output driving a 3.3 volt input can damage it, unless the datasheet states that the pin tolerates 5 volts. In that direction, use a voltage divider for slow signals or a level shifter chip for fast or two-way ones.
Outputs that only pull down

Some outputs are open drain, meaning they can connect the line to ground but cannot drive it high. They rely on a pull-up resistor to bring the line up when released. This allows several devices to share one wire safely, since none can fight another by driving high while it drives low. The I2C bus works this way. If a line of this kind is stuck low or never goes high, a missing pull-up is the first thing to check.
How much a pin can drive

A logic output is a signal source, not a power supply. A typical microcontroller pin can safely source or sink something on the order of 10 to 20 milliamps, with a lower limit on the total across all pins. That is enough for an LED with its resistor and not enough for a motor, a relay coil or a strip of lights. Anything heavier needs a transistor or driver chip between the pin and the load.
Hearing is not listening

In an ordinary conversation, a great deal of attention goes to things other than the speaker. You are planning your reply, judging what was said, recalling a similar story of your own or waiting for a gap. People speak at perhaps 150 words a minute, and the mind works much faster, so there is spare capacity that readily wanders. The speaker usually senses it. Being half heard is among the commonest complaints in marriages and workplaces.
Listening to understand

The psychologist Carl Rogers, working in the 1940s and 50s, argued that the most helpful thing one person can do for another in conversation is to try to grasp the other's meaning from their point of view, without judging it. He and a colleague called this active listening. The listener's task is not to fix, advise or evaluate. It is to understand accurately and to show that they have. Simple as that sounds, few people do it.
Reflecting back

The central technique is to restate what you heard in your own words and check it. So the deadline itself is not the problem, it is that nobody told you it had moved. If you are right, the speaker feels understood and goes further. If you are wrong, they correct you, and you have avoided a misunderstanding. It can feel artificial at first. Done sincerely and not mechanically, it is rarely noticed as a technique at all.
Ask open questions

Questions that can be answered with yes or no shut a conversation down. Questions beginning with what or how open it up. What happened next? How did that affect you? What do you make of it? Be careful with why, which can sound like a demand for justification. A good question follows from what the person has just said, which also proves that you were paying attention. Questions that steer toward your own view are advice in disguise.
Leave silence alone

Most people find a pause of three or four seconds uncomfortable and rush to fill it. Experienced interviewers, counsellors and negotiators do the opposite. When the speaker stops, they wait. Very often the speaker continues, and what comes after the pause is more candid than what came before. Silence signals that you are not in a hurry and that there is room for more. Learning to tolerate it is one of the simplest improvements a listener can make.
Hold the advice

When someone describes a problem, the urge to offer a solution is strong. Frequently they have not asked for one. They may have thought of your suggestion already. They may want to think aloud, or simply to be heard. Jumping to advice can imply that the problem is easy and they should have solved it. If you are unsure what is wanted, ask: would it help to talk through options, or do you mainly want me to listen?
Remove the distractions

Attention is visible. Turning to face someone, looking at them and putting away the phone all communicate that they matter. A phone lying on the table between two people, even untouched, is a reminder that the conversation can be interrupted at any moment. If you truly cannot give someone your attention now, it is better to say so and name a time when you can than to offer a distracted half of it.
What it gets you

People tell good listeners more. They bring bad news earlier, admit mistakes sooner and explain what they actually want. In disputes, being accurately heard often lowers the temperature more than any concession does, since much anger is the frustration of not being understood. Try it once this week. In one conversation, do nothing but ask, reflect and wait. Notice how much longer the other person talks and how much you learn.
The method

Dollar-cost averaging means investing the same sum of money at fixed intervals, whatever the price happens to be. Three hundred dollars on the first of each month into the same fund, for example. You make no attempt to judge whether the market is high or low. The decision is made once and then carried out automatically. Anyone who contributes to a retirement plan from each pay cheque is already doing it.
A built-in advantage

Because the amount is fixed, it buys more units when the price is low and fewer when it is high. Suppose you invest 100 dollars in each of three months at prices of 10, 5 and 10 dollars. You buy 10 units, then 20, then 10. You hold 40 units for 300 dollars, an average cost of 7.50 each. The average price over the period was 8.33. Your cost is lower because your money automatically bought the most when the price was lowest.
The behavioural benefit

The larger advantage is psychological. Investors are tempted to wait for a better moment, to buy after prices have risen and to sell in a panic after they have fallen. An automatic schedule takes those decisions away. A falling market becomes a chance to buy more units for the same money. People who invest by standing order tend to keep going through downturns that drive others out of the market at the worst time.
With a lump sum

A different question arises when you already have a large sum, such as an inheritance. Should you invest it all now or feed it in over a year? A much-cited study by the fund company Vanguard, covering several decades of market history in three countries, found that investing at once did better about two thirds of the time. The reason is simple. Markets rise more often than they fall, so money waiting on the sidelines usually misses some growth.
Why people still phase it in

The remaining third of the time, investing all at once is followed by a fall, and the experience is painful. Spreading a lump sum over several months reduces the chance of that outcome and the regret that comes with it. It costs a little expected return in exchange for a calmer mind. If the alternative to phasing is being too anxious to invest at all, phasing is clearly the better course. Choose a schedule in advance and keep to it.
What it does not do

Dollar-cost averaging does not protect against loss. If the investment falls and stays down, you lose money, having bought all the way down. It does not improve a poor investment. And it works only if you continue during declines, which is when it feels worst and achieves most. Stopping contributions when prices fall throws away the whole advantage of the method.
Making it automatic

The practical value lies in removing yourself from the process. Arrange for the transfer to happen on the day you are paid, before the money can be spent elsewhere. Choose a low-cost, broadly diversified fund. Increase the amount when your income rises. Then look at the account rarely. The fewer decisions you have to take, the fewer opportunities there are to take a bad one.
The bigger picture

Arguments about the best timing involve small differences. How much you save, how long you remain invested and how little you pay in costs matter far more. A person who invests a modest amount every month for thirty years, in good markets and bad, will almost certainly do better than one who spends those years waiting for the ideal moment. A regular habit is unexciting, and that is its strength.
What tilt is

Tilt is the deterioration of your play caused by emotion. The term comes from pinball, where shaking the machine in frustration causes it to lock up. In poker it usually means anger after a bad beat leading to reckless aggression, but it takes many forms. A player on tilt knows the right play and makes the wrong one. Nearly all experienced players agree that it costs them more than any gap in their technical knowledge.
The kinds

Tilt is not only fury. There is the urge to win back losses quickly by playing bigger pots with weaker hands. There is entitlement, the feeling that after so many lost coin flips you are owed a win. There is fear, playing too tightly after a big loss to avoid another. There is boredom, entering pots because you have folded for an hour. And there is overconfidence after a hot streak. Each one pushes your play away from what you know is correct.
Why it happens

The brain's response to a painful loss is the same system that handles physical threat. Heart rate rises, attention narrows, and the urge to act immediately becomes strong. Careful reasoning is exactly what that state suppresses. Poker also delivers punishment for correct play on a regular basis, which is unusual. Getting your money in as a four to one favourite and losing happens one time in five, and each time it feels like an injustice.
Know your triggers

Players tilt in their own characteristic ways. For one it is a particular opponent who talks too much. For another it is being bluffed and shown the cards. For another, losing three hands in a row, or being card-dead for an hour, or making one mistake that they then cannot stop replaying. Write yours down. A trigger you have named in advance is much easier to notice in the moment than one that takes you by surprise.
Catch it early

Tilt is far easier to stop at the first sign than at full strength. Early signs are physical and behavioural: a hot face, a tight jaw, faster breathing, acting quickly, saying something sharp, thinking about a previous hand during the current one. When you notice one, take the simplest step available. Sit out a round. Stand up. Take ten slow breaths. The aim is to interrupt the reaction before it reaches your decisions.
Set limits before you play

Rules made in advance work because they do not depend on judgement in the moment. A stop-loss is a commitment to quit after losing a set number of buy-ins, commonly two or three. A time limit serves the same purpose, since tired players tilt more easily. Some players also set a rule to quit after any hand that makes them visibly angry. The right moment to leave is always earlier than it feels.
Quitting is a skill

The session ends when you say it does, and choosing that moment well is as much a part of the game as any bet. Leaving while behind feels like accepting a loss. But the loss has already occurred, and the only question is whether you play your best from here. If the answer is no, further hands cost money on average. There will always be another game tomorrow, and you will arrive at it with your bankroll and judgement intact.
Outside the game

What you bring to the table affects how you play. Sleep, food, alcohol, stress from work or home, and playing with money you cannot afford to lose all make tilt more likely. Players who treat poker seriously look after the ordinary things for that reason. If you find yourself chasing losses repeatedly, or playing to escape other problems, that goes beyond tilt. Gambling support services exist for exactly that, and using one is a sound decision.
A computer in one package

A microcontroller combines a processor, memory for the program, working memory and a set of input and output circuits on a single chip. It is designed to be embedded in a product and do one job indefinitely: run a washing machine, read a thermostat, blink a bike light. A microprocessor, by contrast, is only the processor and needs separate memory and support chips. A modern car contains dozens of microcontrollers, and a typical home holds hundreds.
The processor core

The core fetches instructions from memory and executes them one after another. Small microcontrollers use simple cores, 8 bits or 32 bits wide, running at a few million to a few hundred million instructions per second. That is slow next to a laptop and more than enough to read a sensor and decide what to do thousands of times a second. The core in the chip at the heart of the classic Arduino Uno is an 8-bit design clocked at 16 megahertz.
Three kinds of memory

Flash memory holds the program and keeps it when power is removed. RAM holds variables while the program runs and is wiped at power-off. Many chips add a small amount of EEPROM for settings that must survive. The quantities are tiny by computer standards. The Arduino Uno's chip has 32 kilobytes of flash and just 2 kilobytes of RAM. Writing software for such a device means being careful with every byte.
Pins that do many jobs

General purpose input and output pins are the chip's contact with the world. Each can be set by software as an input, to read a switch or sensor, or as an output, to drive a signal high or low. Most pins have alternative functions as well, selected in software: a serial port, an analog input, a timer output. This is why the same chip can serve in thousands of different products with only the program changed.
Timers and counters

Hardware timers count clock ticks independently of the main program. They measure intervals, generate precisely timed pulses, produce the pulse-width signals that dim LEDs and steer servo motors, and wake the chip at set times. Because they run in hardware, their timing stays exact even while the processor is busy. A good deal of embedded programming consists of configuring timers correctly, and they are the first peripheral worth learning in depth.
Talking to analog and digital parts

An analog to digital converter turns a voltage on a pin into a number, which is how a microcontroller reads a temperature sensor or a battery level. Serial interfaces let it exchange data with other chips over two to four wires, using standards called UART, SPI and I2C. With those two capabilities, one small chip can read nearly any sensor and control displays, radios, memory cards and motor drivers.
Interrupts and sleep

An interrupt lets an event, such as a pin changing or a timer expiring, pause the main program and run a short routine immediately. This lets the chip respond in microseconds without constantly checking. Combined with sleep modes, in which most of the chip is switched off, it is the key to long battery life. A well-designed sensor node may sleep at a few millionths of an amp and wake for a few thousandths of a second each minute.
Choosing one

For learning, pick a board with good documentation and a large community before worrying about specifications. Classic 8-bit Arduino boards are simple and forgiving. Boards based on 32-bit chips offer far more speed and memory for similar money. Some, such as the ESP32 family, include Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios on the chip. The skills transfer between all of them. Pins, timers, converters and serial ports work on the same principles everywhere.
Know what you want to say

Most muddled writing comes from starting before the writer knows the point. A useful test is to state your message aloud in two sentences to someone who knows nothing about it. If you cannot, the difficulty is not with the prose, and no amount of polishing will cure it. Work out the point first. Much of the labour of writing is discovering what you think, and a first draft is often the place where that happens.
Put the point first

Readers are busy and many stop early. State the conclusion at the beginning, then support it. An email should give its request or its news in the first line. A report should open with what was found and what is recommended. School essays teach people to build toward a conclusion. For nearly every practical purpose the reverse order is better. A reader who stops after one paragraph should still leave with the main message.
Short words, short sentences

Use the plain word when it will serve. Use, not utilize. Start, not commence. Help, not facilitate. Long words chosen to impress make a reader work harder and trust the writer less. Keep most sentences to one idea. If a sentence runs beyond two lines, look for the place where it can be split. Vary the lengths so the rhythm does not become monotonous, but let the short, direct sentence be your default.
Prefer the active voice

In an active sentence, the subject acts: the committee rejected the proposal. In a passive one, the subject is acted upon: the proposal was rejected. The passive is longer and often hides who did what, which is why it is so common in official apologies. It has legitimate uses, when the actor is unknown or unimportant. As a habit, name who did the thing and what they did. Your sentences will be shorter and clearer.
Cut

Nearly every draft is improved by removing a tenth of it. Look for words that add nothing: very, really, quite, in order to, the fact that, it should be noted that. Look for sentences that repeat the previous one in different words. Look for an opening paragraph that merely clears the throat. George Orwell, in a well-known essay on English prose, advised cutting any word that can be cut. Readers never complain that something was too easy to read.
The curse of knowledge

Once you understand something, it is hard to remember not understanding it. In a much-cited experiment, people tapped out the rhythm of a familiar song and predicted that listeners would name it about half the time. Listeners managed it on roughly one attempt in forty. The tappers could hear the melody in their heads. Writers are in the same position. Terms and steps that seem obvious to you may be opaque to a reader.
Be concrete

Abstract statements slide past the reader. Examples stay. Sales rose sharply is weaker than sales rose from 200 to 340 units a month. The policy caused problems is weaker than the policy left three branches without a manager for six weeks. Whenever you make a general claim, follow it with a particular case, a number or a name. If you cannot think of one, consider whether the general claim is true.
Read it aloud

The best single editing technique is to read the draft aloud, or have software read it to you. The ear catches what the eye forgives: the sentence that runs out of breath, the word repeated three times, the phrase that sounds pompous, the step missing from an argument. Wherever you stumble, a reader will too. Leave a draft overnight if you can. In the morning you will read it more nearly as a stranger would.
What a bubble is

A bubble is a sharp rise in the price of an asset that is driven by the expectation of further rises, not by what the asset earns or is used for. People buy because prices are going up, and their buying pushes prices up further. The process sustains itself until new buyers run out. Then prices fall, usually much faster than they rose. Bubbles are easy to identify afterwards and notoriously hard to call at the time.
Tulips

The earliest famous example is from the Dutch Republic in the 1630s. Rare tulip bulbs, especially those with striped petals, became luxury goods, and contracts to buy them changed hands at soaring prices. At the peak, a single prized bulb was reported to cost as much as a fine house. In February 1637 buyers failed to appear at an auction, and the market collapsed within days. Modern historians think the wider economic harm was small and that later moralists exaggerated the tale.
The South Sea

In 1720 the South Sea Company, which held a British trading monopoly of little practical value, offered to take over much of the national debt in exchange for shares. Its share price rose roughly eightfold in a few months, helped by bribes and by lending investors the money to buy. Dozens of imitation companies were floated. By the autumn, the price had collapsed. Among those who lost heavily was Isaac Newton, by then master of the Royal Mint.
Railways and radio

Bubbles often attach to real technological change. In 1840s Britain, investors poured money into railway companies, many of which planned lines that were never built. Shares crashed, yet the country was left with a rail network. In the late 1920s, shares in radio and car companies soared before the crash of 1929. The technology in each case did transform the world. The investors who paid peak prices mostly lost their money all the same.
The dot-com boom

In the late 1990s, the arrival of the internet set off a rush into technology shares. Companies with no profits and little revenue were valued in the billions. The Nasdaq index of American technology shares roughly doubled in the year before its peak in March 2000. Over the next two and a half years it fell by almost 80 percent, and it did not return to that peak for fifteen years. The internet proved even more important than its enthusiasts claimed.
The common pattern

Historians of finance describe a recurring sequence. Something genuinely new appears and creates real profits. Prices rise and attract attention. Credit becomes easy, and people borrow to buy. A story spreads that old rules of value no longer apply. Newcomers with no experience join in, encouraged by neighbours who have made money. Insiders begin to sell. A small shock or simply a pause sets off a rush for the exit.
Why clever people join in

Bubbles do not require stupidity. A professional manager who stays out while prices double will lose clients long before being proved right. Selling early looks like an error for months or years. Many participants know that prices are too high and hope to sell to someone else before the fall. A saying often attributed to the economist John Maynard Keynes holds that a market can stay irrational for longer than an investor can stay solvent.
What an ordinary investor can do

Nobody can reliably time the top, so the defences are structural. Do not borrow to invest in something whose price has recently soared. Be wary when the main argument for buying is that the price has gone up. Be suspicious of any claim that this time the old measures do not apply. Hold a diversified portfolio so that no single enthusiasm can sink you. And accept that you will sometimes watch other people get rich quickly, for a while.
The skill gap is everything

Poker has no house edge between players. Money moves from those who make more mistakes to those who make fewer, minus the fee the room takes. The tenth best player in the world loses money at a table with the top nine. An average player wins steadily at a table of beginners. Improving your own game is slow. Choosing a softer game is immediate, and yet most players sit in the first open seat and never look around.
Signs of a good table

A profitable table has recognizable features. Many players see each flop. Players call the big blind instead of raising. Pots are contested by four or five people. Hands are shown down that should have been folded long before. The mood is lively, with conversation, laughter and drinks. A quiet table of silent players wearing headphones, with most pots won by a single raise before the flop, is a table of regulars and should be avoided.
What to count

You can estimate a table's quality in a few minutes of watching. Count how many players see the flop on average. Three or more suggests a loose, profitable game. Note the size of the average pot relative to the blinds. Watch for anyone who plays almost every hand, since one such player can make a table worth staying at. Online, lobbies often display the percentage of players seeing the flop and the average pot size for each table.
Seat selection

Within a table, some seats are better than others. Because betting moves clockwise, you act after the player on your right in most hands. You want the loose, free-spending players on your right, so that you see what they do before you decide and can isolate them with raises. You want tight, predictable players on your left, since they will seldom interfere. An aggressive, skilled player directly on your left is the worst neighbour, as they will act after you all night.
Ask to move

In most card rooms you can request a table change or a seat change, and nobody will mind. Tell the floor staff you would like to move and they will put you on a list. If a seat opens at your own table that is better placed, you can usually take it by telling the dealer. Few players bother. Those who do are making a decision worth more per hour than nearly any refinement of strategy.
Games change

A table is not fixed in quality. The loose player who made it good may go broke or go home. Two strong regulars may sit down. Check every half hour or so whether the reasons you chose the game still apply. If the table has turned tough, leave, even if you are winning and comfortable. Loyalty to a seat is not rewarded. Good players are restless in this one respect.
Stakes and times

Game quality varies with the clock and the stake. Evenings and weekends bring recreational players. Weekday mornings are dominated by regulars. Holiday periods and the hours around major sporting events are often soft. Moving up in stakes usually means tougher opposition, though not always, and a lively game one level below your usual one can easily be more profitable than a tight game at your normal stake.
Ego is the obstacle

The main reason players ignore all this is pride. Seeking out weak opponents feels less admirable than beating strong ones. But poker pays for results, not for the difficulty of the opposition. Playing against better players has value as a deliberate lesson, paid for knowingly. As a routine, it is a slow way to lose. The most consistently profitable players are rarely the most gifted. They are the ones who are most careful about where they sit.
The idea

Pulse width modulation, or PWM, produces an adjustable average output from a signal that only has two levels. The pin switches between fully on and fully off many times a second. The proportion of each cycle spent on is called the duty cycle. At 25 percent, the pin is on for a quarter of the time. At 75 percent, for three quarters. The load, if it responds slowly compared with the switching, behaves as though it were receiving a steady intermediate level.
The average

The effective voltage is the supply voltage multiplied by the duty cycle. A 5 volt pin at 50 percent averages 2.5 volts. At 20 percent it averages 1 volt. The pin never actually outputs those voltages. It is always at 0 or 5. The averaging is done by the thing being driven: the inertia of a motor, the slow response of a heater, or the human eye watching an LED that is blinking too fast to see.
Why not just lower the voltage

Reducing voltage with a resistor or a linear regulator wastes the difference as heat. PWM avoids that. A transistor that is fully on has almost no voltage across it, and one that is fully off carries no current. In both states it dissipates very little power. Since a PWM switch spends nearly all of its time in one state or the other, almost all the energy reaches the load. This efficiency is the reason PWM is used everywhere.
Frequency matters

The switching rate must be fast enough for the load to smooth it out. For LEDs, anything above a couple of hundred cycles a second looks steady to most people, though higher rates avoid flicker seen in the corner of the eye and on camera. For motors, low frequencies produce an audible whine, so drivers often switch at 20,000 cycles a second or more, above the range of human hearing. The trade-off is that faster switching wastes slightly more power in the transistor.
On a microcontroller

PWM is generated by the chip's hardware timers, so it continues accurately while the program does other things. On the classic Arduino boards, the function that sets it takes a value from 0 to 255, where 0 is always off and 255 is always on, and the default frequency is around 490 cycles a second on most pins. Only certain pins can produce it, and they are usually marked on the board with a small wave symbol.
Driving real loads

A pin can dim a single LED directly through its resistor. Anything larger needs a transistor. The pin's PWM signal drives the gate of a MOSFET, and the MOSFET switches the heavy current for the motor, the lighting strip or the heater. Motors and other coils also need a diode across them to absorb the voltage spike at each switch-off. With that arrangement, a signal of a few milliamps controls a load of many amps.
Servos use it differently

Hobby servo motors read PWM as a command instead of as power. They expect a pulse about fifty times a second, and the width of the pulse sets the position. Roughly one thousandth of a second means one end of travel, two thousandths the other end, and one and a half the centre. The servo's own electronics move the arm to match. Radio control gear and countless robot projects rely on this simple convention.
Turning it into a real voltage

When a true steady voltage is needed, pass the PWM signal through a resistor followed by a capacitor to ground. This filter averages the pulses and leaves a nearly smooth level with a small ripple. It is a cheap way to produce an adjustable reference or control voltage from a chip that has no analog output. For audio or precision work, a dedicated digital to analog converter does better, but the filter is often good enough.
Keep them in proportion

The image of poker as a contest of stares is misleading. The most trustworthy information about an opponent's hand is how they have bet: what they did before the flop, how they sized each bet and how that compares with their usual behaviour. Physical tells are a supplement. Good players use them to tip a decision that is otherwise close, not to overrule the logic of the hand. A player who relies mainly on reading faces will lose to one who reads betting.
Establish a baseline

A behaviour means something only as a departure from what is normal for that person. Some players always talk. Some always sit rigidly still. Some always shuffle their chips. None of that is information until it changes. Spend your first half hour at a table watching how each opponent acts in hands where the cards are eventually shown. Once you know how someone looks and sounds when relaxed, you can notice when they differ.
Weak means strong

A long-standing observation, set out most famously by the writer Mike Caro, is that recreational players act the opposite of what they hold. With a big hand, they sigh, shrug, hesitate and bet as if reluctantly. With a bluff, they bet forcefully, stare the opponent down and try to look confident. The acting is instinctive and often unconscious. Against inexperienced opponents, a display of strength is slightly more likely to mean weakness, and the reverse.
Hands and breathing

Involuntary signs are harder to fake. Trembling hands when placing a large bet usually indicate a very strong hand, not a bluff. It is the release of tension from someone who expects to win a big pot. Bluffers tend to become still, as if trying not to be noticed, and sometimes hold their breath. A player who was chatting and suddenly falls silent after betting, or who freezes when you look at them, is more often bluffing.
Timing

How long someone takes can be as revealing as how they look. An instant call on the flop usually means a draw or a medium hand, since a very strong hand would at least consider raising and a weak one folding. A long pause followed by a bet often means strength dressed up as uncertainty. An instant bet on a card that changes the board often means the player had already decided to bet, which leans toward a bluff. Timing tells also work online.
Glances and chips

Watch opponents as the flop is dealt, not the cards themselves, which will still be there a second later. A player who looks at the flop and then immediately glances at their own chips often liked what they saw and is thinking about betting. A player who stares at the board for a long time has frequently missed. Someone who reaches for chips before you have acted, as if ready to call, is commonly trying to discourage your bet.
Reverse tells

Experienced opponents know all of the above and may act it out deliberately to mislead you. The more skilled the player, the less weight their mannerisms deserve. Against strong opposition, physical reads are close to worthless, and you should return to ranges and bet sizes. The classic tells are most dependable against recreational players who are not thinking about how they appear, which fortunately describes the players from whom most profit comes.
Hiding your own

The simplest defence is uniformity. Take about the same time over every significant decision. Place your chips the same way each time. Look at the same spot on the table after you bet. Say nothing during a hand. You do not need a blank face, sunglasses or a hood. You need a routine that is identical whether you hold the nuts or nothing, so that there is no difference for anyone to observe.
What the converter does

An analog to digital converter, or ADC, measures a voltage and reports it as a whole number. The physical world supplies quantities that vary smoothly. A sensor turns one of them into a voltage. The ADC turns that voltage into a number that a program can compare, store and act upon. Nearly every microcontroller has one built in, connected to several of its pins. It is the route by which any measurement enters a digital system.
Resolution

The number of bits sets how finely the converter divides its range. A 10-bit converter has 1,024 possible output values. A 12-bit one has 4,096. With a range of 0 to 5 volts and 10 bits, each step is about 5 thousandths of a volt. Any change smaller than one step is invisible. With 12 bits over 3.3 volts, each step is under a thousandth of a volt. More bits mean finer detail, up to the point where electrical noise swamps the last few.
The reference voltage

An ADC does not measure in volts. It measures the input as a fraction of a reference voltage. A reading of 512 on a 10-bit converter means the input is half the reference, whatever that is. If the reference is the 5 volt supply and the supply is actually 4.8 volts, every reading is off by 4 percent. Accurate work uses a dedicated, stable reference. Many chips include an internal one that can be selected in software.
Sampling in time

The converter takes snapshots, called samples, at intervals. To capture a signal faithfully, it must sample more than twice as fast as the highest frequency present. This is the Nyquist rule. Sample too slowly and fast signals masquerade as slow ones, an error called aliasing, which cannot be removed afterwards. Compact discs use about 44,000 samples a second because human hearing reaches about 20,000 cycles a second. A room thermometer needs one sample every few seconds.
Filter before you sample

Because aliasing cannot be undone, signals are filtered before they reach the converter to remove frequencies above half the sampling rate. A resistor and a capacitor are often enough. The capacitor has a second benefit. Many converters take a brief gulp of current from the input at the moment of sampling, and a small capacitor right at the pin supplies it. Without one, a sensor with high output resistance gives readings that are low and erratic.
Noise and averaging

Readings from a real ADC jitter by a few counts even when the input is steady, because of electrical noise from the supply, nearby digital signals and the converter itself. Taking several readings and averaging them reduces the jitter. Sixteen samples averaged typically give a far steadier result than one. Keeping analog wiring short and away from fast digital lines helps as well. Some chips let the processor sleep briefly while converting, to quieten things down.
Scaling the answer

The raw count is rarely what you want. To get a voltage, multiply the count by the reference voltage and divide by the number of steps. To get a temperature or a pressure, apply the sensor's own formula from its datasheet. Signals larger than the reference must be reduced first with a voltage divider, and very small ones amplified with an op-amp so that they use more of the available range.
When the built-in one is not enough

Internal converters are convenient and adequate for most tasks. Weighing scales, precision thermometers and audio need more. External converter chips offer 16 to 24 bits, very low noise and built-in amplification, and they pass their readings to the microcontroller over a serial bus. For most hobby projects, the limiting factor is the sensor and the wiring long before it is the resolution of the converter.
What your chips are

In a cash game, chips are money. A 5 dollar chip is worth 5 dollars, and you may leave with your stack whenever you wish. In a tournament, you pay an entry fee and receive chips that have no cash value. You play until you lose them all or win everyone else's. Prizes are paid according to the order in which players are eliminated. This one difference changes the correct play in a great many situations.
The blinds rise

In a cash game, the blinds never change, and stacks are typically deep, a hundred big blinds or more. In a tournament, the blinds increase at set intervals. A stack that was comfortable an hour ago becomes short without your losing a hand. Much tournament play therefore happens with 20 to 40 big blinds, and a good deal with fewer than 15. Deep-stacked skills matter early. Short-stacked skills decide who wins.
Survival has value

In a cash game, if you lose your stack you can buy another, so only the expected value in chips matters. In a standard tournament, once your chips are gone, you are out. Being alive has a value of its own, because it keeps open the chance of reaching the prizes. This makes some gambles that would be correct in a cash game incorrect in a tournament, particularly near the point where the prizes begin.
The prize structure

A typical tournament pays about the top 10 to 15 percent of the field. Most of the prize money is concentrated in the last few places, with first often receiving a fifth or more of the pool. Scraping into the lowest prizes returns little more than the entry fee. The real money is at the final table. Good tournament players do not aim merely to survive into the prizes. They accumulate chips so that they can contend for the top spots.
Variance

The swings in tournaments are far larger than in cash games. Even a very good tournament player reaches the prizes in only a minority of events, perhaps one in six or seven, and wins outright very rarely. Long runs without a meaningful result are normal. This is why the bankroll recommended for tournaments, counted in buy-ins, is several times that for cash games, and why results over a few dozen events tell you almost nothing about your skill.
Stack size in big blinds

Tournament players think of their stack as a number of big blinds, not as a count of chips. With more than 40, you can play a full range of moves. Between 20 and 40, calling raises with speculative hands becomes costly, and reraising all in becomes a major weapon. Below about 12, the game simplifies to moving all in or folding. Recognizing which zone you and your opponents are in is the foundation of tournament strategy.
Antes

Most tournaments add an ante after the early levels: a small forced payment from every player, or one larger payment from the big blind, on each hand. Antes make the starting pot bigger, which makes stealing it more rewarding and defending it more justified. Correct play becomes noticeably looser and more aggressive once they begin. Players who keep to the tight style suited to the early levels are slowly drained.
Which to choose

Cash games suit people who want to play for a fixed time, leave when they like and see steadier results. Tournaments offer a large potential prize for a small fixed risk, a clear beginning and end, and long stretches of disappointment. They can last many hours with no option to stop early. Many players enjoy both. It helps to remember which one you are in, since instincts trained in one are often wrong in the other.
Why serial

Sending eight bits at once would need eight wires. Sending them one after another needs only one or two. Serial communication trades a little speed for far fewer pins and connections, which is nearly always worthwhile. Three serial standards dominate small electronics. They have been in use for decades, and almost every sensor, display and memory chip you can buy speaks at least one of them.
UART: two wires, no clock

The oldest and simplest is the UART. It uses one wire to transmit and one to receive, plus a shared ground. There is no clock signal. Both sides must agree in advance on the speed, called the baud rate, such as 9,600 or 115,200 bits a second. Each byte is framed by a start bit and a stop bit so that the receiver can find its edges. The transmit pin of one device connects to the receive pin of the other.
Where UART is used

A UART connects exactly two devices. It is the usual link between a microcontroller and a computer for uploading programs and printing debugging messages, and it is how many GPS receivers, Bluetooth modules and other self-contained units send their data. Its common failure modes are simple. Either the two wires are not crossed over, or the two sides are set to different speeds, which produces a stream of garbage characters.
I2C: two wires, many devices

I2C was developed by Philips in the early 1980s to connect chips inside televisions. It uses two wires shared by every device on the bus: one for data and one for a clock. Each device has an address, and the controller begins every message by naming the device it wants. Dozens of sensors can hang on the same pair of wires. Standard speed is 100,000 bits a second, with faster modes available.
The pull-ups on I2C

I2C devices can only pull the lines low. Resistors connected to the supply pull them high again when released. Without those pull-up resistors, nothing works. Values of a few kilohms are typical. Many breakout boards include them, and when several boards are joined, their resistors combine in parallel, which occasionally causes trouble. The other common problem is two chips with the same fixed address, since each address on a bus must be unique.
SPI: more wires, more speed

SPI, which originated at Motorola, uses a clock line, a data line in each direction and a separate select line for each device. The controller pulls one select line low to choose which device it is addressing. With no addresses and no pull-ups, signals are driven hard in both directions and speeds of millions of bits a second are routine. The cost is pins. Every additional device needs its own select line.
Choosing between them

The decision is usually made by the part you want to use. Sensors that produce a few numbers at a time, such as temperature, pressure and motion chips, commonly use I2C, since the bus is tidy and speed is unimportant. Parts that move a lot of data, such as displays, memory cards and radio modules, use SPI. Anything that is a module with its own processor, or a link to a computer, tends to use a UART.
Seeing the conversation

When a serial link misbehaves, guessing is slow. An inexpensive logic analyser, which records the signals and decodes them into bytes on a computer screen, shows at once whether anything is being sent, whether the device acknowledges and what the data contain. It is among the most useful tools for digital work. Before reaching for one, check the three usual causes: wrong wiring, wrong voltage level and a missing ground connection between the two boards.
The independent chip model

In a tournament, the value of your stack is your share of the prize pool on average, given all the stacks. The standard way to estimate it is the independent chip model, known as ICM. It assumes each player's chance of finishing first equals their share of the chips, then works out second place among the rest in the same way, and so on. The result converts a chip stack into an expected prize in money.
A three-player example

Three players remain with 1,000 chips each. The prizes are 50, 30 and 20 dollars. By symmetry, each stack is worth 33.33 dollars. Now two of them go all in against each other and one is eliminated. The loser collects third prize, 20 dollars. The winner has 2,000 chips against the remaining player's 1,000 and, by the model, an expected prize of 43.33 dollars. The player who sat out now has an expectation of 36.67.
What the example shows

Look at the changes. The winner doubled their chips and their prize expectation rose by 10 dollars, from 33.33 to 43.33. The loser's fell by 13.33. The player who folded and watched gained 3.33 for doing nothing. Doubling your stack did not double its value. This is the central fact of tournament endgames. Chips you might lose are worth more than the same number of chips you might win.
The risk premium

In the example, calling an all-in bet risks 13.33 dollars of value to gain 10. To break even you must win about 57 percent of the time, though in chips alone 50 percent would do. That extra requirement is sometimes called the risk premium. It means you should fold some hands that would be clear calls in a cash game. The more unequal the stacks and the steeper the payouts, the larger the premium becomes.
The bubble

The effect is strongest on the bubble, the stage when one more elimination puts everyone left into the prizes. The player eliminated then has played for hours for nothing. Medium stacks have the most to lose and should play tightly, avoiding confrontations with stacks that could knock them out. A very short stack has less to protect and must take chances. The biggest stack can exploit all of this ruthlessly.
The big stack's licence

A chip leader on the bubble can raise very frequently, because the players behind cannot call without risking their tournament. Opponents with medium stacks are forced to fold good hands. Big stacks often add substantially to their chips during this stage without showing a single hand. If you are that big stack, raise relentlessly into the medium stacks. If you are a medium stack, accept that you are being robbed and wait, unless you hold a hand strong enough to justify the risk.
Fold when others are about to bust

The model produces advice that feels unnatural. If you have a medium stack and a much shorter one is about to be forced all in by the blinds, folding almost everything is correct, since their elimination raises your prize expectation for free. Calling an all-in with a hand that is a small favourite can be a mistake. In extreme cases, late in satellite tournaments where every remaining prize is identical, folding a pair of aces before the flop can be right.
Do not overdo it

ICM is about the late stages. Early in a tournament, with the prizes far away, the difference between chips and money is small, and you should play to accumulate. Players who learn about ICM sometimes become too cautious everywhere and fold their way into small prizes without ever contending for large ones. Free calculators let you enter stacks and payouts to see the figures. An hour with one builds a sound feel for when survival should outweigh chips.
What happens inside a switch

When you press a button, two pieces of metal come together. They do not meet and stay met. They collide, spring apart and collide again, several times, before settling. The same happens on release. This chatter is called contact bounce. It typically lasts from under a thousandth of a second to a few hundredths, depending on the switch. To a person, the press feels like a single event. Electrically, it is a rapid burst of connections and disconnections.
Why it matters

A microcontroller can check a pin millions of times a second. It sees each bounce as a separate press. A program that counts presses will jump by three or seven on a single push. A button meant to toggle a light will leave it in a random state. Old electromechanical circuits were too slow to notice. Anything digital is fast enough to be fooled, so every design that reads a mechanical contact must deal with it.
The simplest software fix

The most common remedy is a short wait. When the program first sees the pin change, it pauses for 20 to 50 thousandths of a second and then looks again. If the pin is still in the new state, the press is treated as genuine. By then the contacts have settled. The delay is far too short for a person to notice. Its drawback is that a plain pause stops the program from doing anything else for that time.
A better software method

A more refined approach avoids pausing. The program notes the time whenever the raw reading changes. Only when the reading has remained the same for longer than a set interval does it accept the new state. Meanwhile the rest of the program carries on. Another version samples the pin at a regular interval from a timer and requires several identical samples in a row. Both are short pieces of code and are found in ready-made libraries.
Act on the change, not the level

A related mistake is acting for as long as the button is held, when the intent was to act once per press. The program should compare the current debounced state with the previous one and respond only at the moment it changes from released to pressed. This is called edge detection. Combined with debouncing, it gives exactly one action for each push, however long the finger stays on the button.
Hardware debouncing

The alternative is to clean the signal before it reaches the chip. A resistor and a capacitor at the switch slow the voltage so that the brief bounces are smoothed over. Because the result rises and falls gradually, it is passed through a gate with hysteresis, known as a Schmitt trigger, which snaps cleanly between states. Many microcontroller inputs have this built in. Hardware debouncing is preferred when the switch triggers an interrupt.
Bounce and interrupts

Interrupts respond to a pin change within millionths of a second, so a bouncing switch can fire the routine many times in succession. Handling this in software means recording the time of the last accepted interrupt and ignoring any that follow within a few hundredths of a second. For buttons pressed by people, simply checking the pin regularly from the main program is usually easier and perfectly adequate. Interrupts are better saved for signals that are fast and clean.
Not only buttons

Any mechanical contact bounces: relays, limit switches, rotary encoders, reed switches triggered by magnets, tilt sensors. Rotary encoders are especially troublesome, since their contacts are small and they produce many transitions in each turn. If a count drifts, a menu skips entries or a counter races ahead, suspect bounce before suspecting the logic. Looking at the signal on an oscilloscope settles it at once and shows how long the settling takes.
Why the choice narrows

Suppose you have ten big blinds and raise to two and a half. You have put a quarter of your stack in. If someone reraises, you are getting such a good price that you can hardly fold. If you are called, the pot after the flop is more than half your remaining chips, and one bet commits you. Since you will rarely be able to fold later, the sound course is to put everything in at once or put in nothing.
The power of the shove

Moving all in before the flop has two ways to win. Everyone may fold, in which case you collect the blinds and antes, typically adding a quarter or more to a ten big blind stack with no risk. Or you may be called, in which case you still have a chance, usually between 30 and 45 percent even with a modest hand. The combination makes shoving profitable with a much wider range of hands than most players expect.
Calling is harder than pushing

A long-established principle is that you need a stronger hand to call an all-in than to make one. The player who shoves can win by a fold. The player who calls can only win at showdown and is up against a range that was chosen to be shoved. So the ranges are lopsided. From the small blind with ten big blinds, pushing more than half of all hands is correct. The big blind should call with considerably fewer.
Position and stack size

The earlier your seat, the more players remain who could wake up with a strong hand, so the tighter your shoving range must be. Under the gun at a full table with ten big blinds, you might shove only pairs, big aces and the best suited broadway cards. On the button, with two players left to act, roughly a third or more of all hands qualify. As your stack shrinks from twelve big blinds toward six, the ranges widen further from every seat.
Which hands hold up

When you are called, you will usually be behind, so the hands worth shoving are those that still do reasonably well against a calling range. Any ace is valuable because it is seldom far behind. Pairs are strong, since they are at least a coin flip against two higher cards. Suited connected cards do better than they look, because they are rarely dominated. The hands to avoid are weak offsuit kings and queens, which callers so often have beaten.
Do not wait too long

The commonest error is waiting for a premium hand while the stack dwindles. With ten big blinds, a shove makes most opponents fold. With four, calling costs them so little that almost anyone will call with almost anything, and you must then win a showdown. The fold equity has gone. Each round of blinds also costs a large part of a short stack. It is better to shove a mediocre hand with eight big blinds than to wait for a good one with three.
Being first in

Nearly all of this applies when everyone before you has folded. If someone has already raised, you are no longer stealing. You are calling their raise with your stack, and you need a far better hand, since their range is strong and they are unlikely to fold. Shoving over a raise is sound with good pairs and big aces, or against a player who raises very loosely. Being the first player to enter the pot is what gives the short stack its power.
Learn the charts

Mathematicians have worked out the ranges at which neither the shover nor the caller can do better by changing strategy, and they are published as push or fold charts. A chart shows, for each seat and stack size, exactly which hands to shove. Memorizing the broad pattern takes an evening. Because so many tournament hands are played at these stack sizes, few areas of study give a faster return.
Why regulation is needed

A battery's voltage falls as it discharges. A wall adapter's output varies with the load. Chips, meanwhile, need a supply that stays within a few percent of 5 or 3.3 volts. A regulator sits between the two, taking a varying input and delivering a fixed output. Nearly every electronic device contains at least one. The choice of type affects efficiency, heat, size, cost and electrical noise.
How a linear regulator works

A linear regulator behaves like an automatically adjusted resistor in series with the load. It compares its output with an internal reference and continuously varies its resistance to hold the output steady. The familiar three-legged 7805 turns anything from about 7 to 25 volts into 5. Linear regulators need only a couple of small capacitors, cost very little and produce an exceptionally clean, quiet output.
The price is heat

The surplus voltage is burned off. The power wasted equals the voltage dropped across the regulator multiplied by the current. Dropping 12 volts to 5 while supplying half an amp wastes three and a half watts, more than the two and a half delivered. Efficiency in that case is about 42 percent. The regulator needs a heatsink or it will overheat and shut itself down. Linear regulators suit low currents or small differences between input and output.
Dropout

A linear regulator needs its input to exceed its output by a minimum margin, called the dropout voltage. For the classic 7805 it is about 2 volts, so it cannot make 5 volts from a 6 volt battery pack. Low dropout regulators, usually abbreviated LDO, manage with a few tenths of a volt or less. They are standard in battery-powered devices, where they can keep regulating until the battery is nearly exhausted.
How a switching regulator works

A switching regulator does not burn the excess. It chops the input on and off at high speed and uses an inductor and a capacitor to smooth the result, adjusting the on time to hold the output steady. Because the switch is always fully on or fully off, little energy is lost. Efficiencies of 85 to 95 percent are normal. A version that lowers voltage is a buck converter. One that raises it is a boost converter.
The trade-offs

Switching regulators are more complicated. They need an inductor, careful layout and more parts. Their output carries a small ripple at the switching frequency, and the fast edges radiate electrical noise that can disturb radio receivers and sensitive measurements. Ready-made modules have made them easy to use, and they are now cheap. For anything drawing real current from a higher voltage, such as running a 5 volt board from a 12 volt battery, a switching regulator is the sensible choice.
Using both together

Many designs combine the two. A switching regulator does the heavy work of bringing a high voltage down efficiently to a little above the target. A linear regulator then removes the ripple and supplies clean power to sensitive analog or radio circuits. The linear stage drops very little voltage, so it wastes very little. This arrangement gives nearly the efficiency of one and the quietness of the other.
Choosing

Ask three questions. How much current will the load draw? How far apart are the input and output voltages? How sensitive is the circuit to noise? Multiply the voltage difference by the current. If the result is under about half a watt, a linear regulator is simple and adequate. Above that, heat becomes a problem and a switching type is preferable. Whichever you use, fit the input and output capacitors the datasheet specifies, placed close to the regulator.
An unbeatable strategy

Game theory shows that poker has an equilibrium: a strategy which, if you follow it, cannot be beaten in the long run by any counter-strategy. Players call it GTO, for game theory optimal. It mixes value bets and bluffs, calls and folds, in proportions such that an opponent gains nothing by adjusting. If they deviate from their own equilibrium play, they lose money to you automatically, without your needing to notice what they are doing wrong.
How it is found

No human can calculate equilibrium play at the table. Computer programs called solvers approximate it by playing a simplified version of a situation against themselves many millions of times, adjusting until neither side can improve. They became widely available to players around the middle of the 2010s and transformed the study of the game. In 2017 a program beat a team of leading professionals at two-player no-limit hold'em, and in 2019 another beat professionals at six-player tables.
What solvers taught

Some lessons surprised even experts. Solvers bet small with a wide range on many flops, where humans had bet large with a narrow one. They check strong hands more than people did. They use very large bets in spots where the opponent cannot hold the best hands. They defend their blinds with a wider range than had been considered correct. Much of what is now standard advice came from watching what the machines did and working out why.
The limits of balance

Equilibrium play guarantees you will not lose to anyone. It does not guarantee you will win as much as possible. Against an opponent who calls far too often, the equilibrium strategy still bluffs at its usual rate and gives money away. It profits from their errors only passively. A strategy designed for a perfect adversary leaves a great deal on the table when the adversary is a tourist who has not folded a pair all evening.
Exploitative play

The alternative is to depart from balance deliberately in order to attack a known weakness. If a player folds too much, bluff them relentlessly. If they call too much, never bluff and bet your good hands bigger. If they only raise with the nuts, fold to their raises without regret. This is exploitative play. Against weak or predictable opponents it earns far more than equilibrium play does, which is why it is the main source of profit in most real games.
The risk

Every exploit opens you to a counter. If you bluff constantly because someone folds too often, and they notice and begin calling, you lose heavily until you adjust back. Against unobservant opponents, this hardly matters. Against good ones, it does. The larger your departure from balance, the more it earns while it works and the more it costs when it is detected. You are betting that you understand your opponent better than they understand you.
How good players combine them

The practical approach is to use equilibrium play as a baseline and exploitation as an adjustment. Against unknown or strong opponents, stay near the baseline, where you cannot be hurt much. As you gather evidence of specific mistakes, move away from it in the direction that punishes them, by an amount proportional to your confidence. Knowing roughly what balanced play looks like is what allows you to recognize how an opponent is deviating from it.
What to study

For most players, the best return comes from learning the broad shapes of sound play: which hands to open from each seat, how to size bets on different boards, how often to defend. Then spend your attention at the table on observing how actual opponents differ from that. Memorizing precise solver frequencies is a matter for professionals facing other professionals. Below that level, the largest edge lies in noticing mistakes and adjusting to them.
The supply is not perfect

On a schematic, the power rail is a line with the same voltage everywhere. On a real board, it is a length of copper with resistance and, more importantly, inductance. Inductance resists rapid changes in current. When a chip suddenly demands a burst of current, as digital chips do every time they switch, the supply cannot deliver it instantly through the wiring. The voltage at the chip's power pin dips for a moment.
What the capacitor does

A small capacitor placed right at the chip's power pins acts as a local reservoir. When the chip demands a sudden burst, the capacitor supplies it at once from a few millimetres away. It then refills from the main supply at leisure. The supply voltage at the chip stays steady. This is called decoupling or bypassing, because it isolates each chip's rapid demands from the rest of the circuit.
The standard recipe
